newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Rash of killings shake Tajikistan's frail peace.
newsitem.headline: Rash of killings shake Tajikistan's frail peace.

text.p: Gunmen have killed seven people, including a Russian serviceman and two Russians employed by the U.S. embassy, in a spate of attacks in the Tajik capital a day after the end of a two-week international hostage crisis.
Unidentified assailants attacked various residential areas in the west of the city on Tuesday night.
Five of those shot were ethnic Russians, including one woman. A local scientist of Uzbek origin and a Tajik policeman were also killed, an interior ministry spokesman said.

Both Moscow and the U.S embassy in Dushanbe issued statements condemning the attacks, the most serious recent outbreak of violence in the volatile Central Asian State, which is still tense after a four-year civil war.
"There is a clear anti-Russian direction to these acts of banditry," said a Russian Foreign Ministry statement, calling for the gunmen to be brought to justice.
"There can be no justification for these brutal murders" said a U.S. embassy statement, which also demanded that the Tajik government act as quickly as possible to catch and punish the perpetrators.

No one has claimed responsibility for the attacks but they have been widely blamed on fighters of the Islamist opposition who have battled the former Soviet republic's secular government over the past four years.

Russian soldiers stationed in Tajikistan have often come under fire from the country's Islamist guerrillas but only two of the latest ethnic Russian victims served with Russian troops. They were border guards and one was killed with his girlfriend.
Two other Russian victims were security workers at the U.S. embassy in Dushanbe who were dressed in distinctive uniforms with special badges and sleeve chevrons with U.S. flags.
"We are worried. The two security workers did not look like Russian army servicemen, and this is the largest number of such killings I can remember," a Western diplomat in Dushanbe said.
A Tajik policeman was also killed in an attack on a psychiatric hospital he was guarding. The attackers freed one of the patients, Nazhmetdin Alimov, who belonged to a group fighting the government.

The killings ocurred just a day after the end of a 14-day hostage crisis that highlighted the instability of Tajikistan, an impoverished former Soviet republic bordering China and Afghanistan. Russian and Western hostages were held by a rebel group in a standoff with the government.

Moscow said the latest murders mirrored a series of attacks at the end of December and beginning of January and were aimed at destroying the fragile peace established at the end of last year between the government and the united Islamist opposition.
"The organisers and executors want to complicate the situation in the country and block the process of political settlement under way in Tajikistan," the Russian Foreign Ministry statement said.
Russia leads a force of about 20,000 peacekeepers and borderguards in the former Soviet republic, which it regards as a bulwark against the spread of militant Islam on its vulnerable southern flank.
Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov and opposition leader Sayid Abdullo Nuri are expected to hold talks on Thursday in Iran to pave the way for a meeting in Moscow on February 26.

The ceasefire between Rakhmonov's secular government and the united Islamist opposition agreed last December seems to be holding but the relative stability is often disturbed by acts of terrorism like hostage-taking or night killings in Dushanbe.

Foreign experts say Rakhmonov's grip on Tajikistan is very tenuous and propped up by Russia's military force. They say he controls only some 20 percent of the mountainous country, with another half controlled by various rebel groups.
